title: South Africa’s estimated 21bn-litre fuel market is dominated by road demand
side: All values: bn litres. Allocations are estimates; manufacturing is an industry residual.
takeaway: Demand is estimated at 20.99bn litres in 2025; road uses account for most allocated demand.
source: Department annual sales, 2013–2023. Estimated 2024–2025: analytical workbook v02. The Department series is used consistently. Segment split: analytical workbook v02, Segments. Displayed figures rounded; other diesel remains unallocated.

title: Agricultural fuel demand rebounds while mining and manufacturing remain broadly flat
side: Manufacturing covers the energy-balance industry residual, not a complete industrial census.
takeaway: Sector activity produces different demand paths; applying one GDP growth rate would hide these differences.
source: Stats SA mining/manufacturing indices and agriculture real GVA; mean 2018–2021 fuel intensity. Sector diesel values after 2021 are estimates.

title: Eskom’s fuel use fell by 40% in FY2025 as electricity supply improved
side: Eskom: 1.130bn L in FY2024 → 0.679bn L in FY2025 (diesel + kerosene).
2025 utility + private power estimate: 1.08bn L, including 0.20bn L assumed private backup.
IPP conversion and fiscal-year proxies are estimates; private use is not measured by Eskom.
takeaway: Improved electricity supply reduces peaking and backup fuel use; the private-backup contribution remains estimated.
source: Eskom Integrated Report 2025, p141. Fiscal years end in March. Reported series includes diesel and kerosene; private backup consumption is outside this series. Analytical workbook v02, Segments: IPP conversion and private-backup assumptions.

title: Rail volumes are recovering, creating scope to reduce road diesel use
side: Rail: 160.7m tonnes in 2024 to 168.3m in 2025. Road: 979.8m to 976.5m tonnes.
A shift of mining, agricultural and manufactured goods to rail can reduce truck fuel use.
Rail growth alone does not prove road displacement; distance, cargo and traction mix matter.
takeaway: Road remains the dominant freight mode; sustained rail recovery could change the diesel required to move goods.
source: Stats SA P7162 December 2025 p7; all reported freight. Analytical workbook v02, Evidence.

title: Hybrids dominate electrified new-vehicle sales; fleet fuel savings emerge as vehicles turn over
side: BEV: 1,088 sales, or 0.18% of all new vehicles.
PHEVs and conventional hybrids still consume fuel; savings depend on usage.
New sales are not fleet penetration. Efficiency and mileage must be modelled separately.
takeaway: The model’s fuel-efficiency path is a planning assumption; new-vehicle sales alone do not quantify national fuel savings.
source: naamsa all-market sales 2025; master workbook Vehicle history S31:S36; evidence retained in market story v27 p11. Analytical workbook v02: efficiency is a planning assumption; avoid double-counting hybrid savings.

title: Changes in refinery output alter the volume that imports must supply
rows: Secunda
Refined-products output: 29.1m barrels in FY2024; 27.6m in FY2025; 30.6m in FY2026
Operating recovery can increase domestic supply; petrol and diesel yields determine import displacement.
Natref
Sasol-reported output: 17.8m barrels in FY2024; 14.7m in FY2025; 25.8m in FY2026
FY2026 includes above-share production, so the latest reported change cannot be treated as a like-for-like change in whole-plant output.
Astron
Reported refined products: 166,204 billion Btu in 2024; 164,365 billion Btu in 2025
Output and product mix affect supply; energy units require conversion before comparison with customs litres.
SAPREF and PetroSA
No refining contribution included in the 2025 production assessment
Restored refining would displace imports only when plants produce saleable products. Terminal handling is not refinery output.
takeaway: The 5.8bn-litre 2025 petrol/diesel baseline is a planning assumption; these differently scoped plant disclosures do not sum directly to it.
source: Sasol production metrics FY2025 and FY2026; Glencore annual reports 2024 and 2025; 2025 plant assessment. Fiscal and calendar periods and reporting scopes differ. Product yields and reporting scopes require reconciliation to the 5.8bn-litre planning baseline.

title: Durban’s inland share depends on competing gateways and reliable onward connections
rows: Durban and other SA ports
Durban customs: 13.16bn L of petrol/diesel imports in 2025
Allocate national imports across gateways before assessing inland customer reach.
Durban–NMPP–Lesedi
Existing coastal-to-inland connection; customer and product access remain to be established
Pipeline, receipt and dispatch constraints determine the flows Vopak can serve.
Matola infrastructure
Galp/IPG: 60,000m³ petrol/diesel storage; Petromoc: 390,000m³ across liquid fuels
Do not add potentially overlapping capacities or equate tankage with annual SA deliveries.
Observed Mozambique route
Komatipoort recorded imports: 0.303bn L in 2022 → 0.086bn L in 2025
Observed cross-border flows provide a firmer volume anchor than storage capacity.
Walvis Bay alternative
Comparable delivered-cost, access and SA flow evidence is not established in this review
Retain as a route to assess; no quantified diversion or customer capture is assigned.
takeaway: Compare the same product and inland destination across routes; Matola and Walvis Bay affect gateway share, not national demand.
source: SARS customs 2022/2025; Galp Matola commissioning, 3 December 2020; Petromoc logistics; existing Durban–Lesedi corridor evidence in market-sizing workbook. Walvis Bay diversion is unquantified; comparable delivered-cost evidence remains open.
